strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Map how agents fail during extended, multi-step tasks and determine which failures are detectable, recoverable, or silently corrupt later results. Examine incorrect reasoning and plans, tool misuse, incomplete observations, stale or compressed context, instruction misunderstandings, environmental changes, and accumulated state errors. Trace concrete failure chains from initiating fault through subsequent actions to user-visible consequences; distinguish model limitations from architecture, orchestration, memory, interface, and environment failures. Investigate detection of silent errors, calibrated uncertainty versus actual failure, retry and replanning policies, escalation, and safe termination. Analyze checkpointing, state reconstruction, independent verification, rollback, idempotency, and human intervention as recovery mechanisms. For each mechanism, specify assumptions, failure modes, and measurable recovery criteria; compare recovery against restarting and continuing without intervention. Develop fault-injection scenarios and trace-based analyses that reveal propagation and test whether recovery restores correct state rather than merely producing a plausible answer. Deliver a failure taxonomy, causal workflow maps, and a prioritized set of falsifiable experiments, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

pending_investigation.claim: In an explicit partial-commit model, adding one retry can increase acknowledged completion while decreasing actual task correctness. If an attempt applies an operation and returns an acknowledgment with probability a, applies it but loses the acknowledgment with probability b, and does nothing and times out with probability c, then retrying once after a timeout changes the probability of exactly one applied operation by (a+b)(c-b). Thus, when b>c and a+b>0, retries reduce correctness despite increasing acknowledged completion whenever 0<a<1. This is a conditional analytical counterexample, not an empirical finding about deployed agents.
pending_investigation.method: Analyze a minimal state-changing tool task: apply exactly one debit. Compare three architectures: no retry; one retry after timeout without deduplication; and the same retry policy with atomic, durable server-side idempotency. Derive the terminal outcomes by exhaustive case analysis. Hypothesis: acknowledgment-based evaluation can rank a retry mechanism above a baseline even when an independent ledger oracle ranks it below. The discriminating experiment would inject separately controlled pre-commit failures and post-commit acknowledgment losses, randomize architectures across isolated task instances, and compare acknowledgment, ledger correctness, duplicate effects, latency, and cost. The calculation assumes independent identically distributed attempt outcomes, reliable acknowledgments, no concurrent writers, and no compensating operations. No experiment was executed; both supplied computational runtimes are unavailable.

reasoning_steps.title: Define task correctness separately from reported completion
reasoning_steps.argument: Let N be the number of applied debits for one logical request. Actual correctness is Y=1 exactly when N=1, regardless of what the agent reports. Reported completion is R=1 when the agent receives at least one valid acknowledgment. N=0 is omission; N>=2 is duplication. A read-only oracle inspecting an authoritative ledger can evaluate Y after execution. This deliberately narrow task makes the correctness predicate explicit rather than treating fluent completion reports as evidence.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the failure model and baseline
reasoning_steps.argument: Each attempted invocation has one of three mutually exclusive outcomes: A, one operation applied and acknowledged, with probability a; B, one operation applied but acknowledgment lost, with probability b; C, no operation applied and timeout, with probability c. Here a,b,c>=0 and a+b+c=1. Outcomes of successive invocations are independent with the same probabilities. The baseline invokes once. Therefore P(Y=1)=a+b, P(R=1)=a, and duplicate probability is zero. A B outcome is a correct external state with unresolved client knowledge, not a false claim of completion.

reasoning_steps.title: Enumerate the non-idempotent retry outcomes
reasoning_steps.argument: The retry policy stops after A and invokes once more after B or C. Its terminal paths are A, BA, BB, BC, CA, CB, and CC, with probabilities a, ba, b², bc, ca, cb, and c². These exhaust all outcomes because their sum is a+(b+c)(a+b+c)=1. Exactly one operation occurs on A, BC, CA, and CB. Two operations occur on BA and BB. No operation occurs on CC. Acknowledgment occurs on A, BA, and CA.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the ranking reversal and its boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: For the retry policy, P(Y=1)=a+ca+2bc, P(R=1)=a+(b+c)a=a(2-a), and P(N>=2)=b(a+b). Subtracting baseline correctness gives a+ca+2bc-(a+b)=(a+b)(c-b). Thus retries harm correctness when post-commit acknowledgment loss is more frequent than pre-commit failure, provided a+b>0. Reported completion increases by a(1-a), strictly positive for 0<a<1. The formulas also cover edge cases: b=c gives no correctness change; a=1 causes no retry; c=1 leaves correctness zero. No claim follows that retries are generally harmful outside these assumptions.

reasoning_steps.title: Give a concrete analytical counterexample
reasoning_steps.argument: Set a=7/10, b=2/10, c=1/10. The baseline has actual correctness 0.90 and acknowledged completion 0.70. One non-idempotent retry has actual correctness 0.81, acknowledged completion 0.91, duplicate probability 0.18, and omission probability 0.01. Its probability of acknowledged but incorrect completion is P(BA)=0.14. Expected invocation count rises from 1 to 1+(b+c)=1.30. These numbers are substitutions into the proved formulas, not simulated or observed rates. They show a 21-percentage-point gain in acknowledged completion alongside a 9-percentage-point loss in actual correctness.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify the invariant needed for the revised architecture
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose every retry carries the same logical operation key and payload, and a server atomically and durably records that key together with its effect. Repeated accepted requests for the key return the prior result without applying another debit. Within the same A/B/C transport model, interpret A and B as acceptance of the logical operation, either initially or by retrieving its prior result. This invariant ensures N<=1. Under the retry policy N=0 only on CC, so P(Y=1)=1-c², while P(R=1)=a(2-a) remains unchanged. For the example, correctness is 0.99 and duplication is zero. A key in the client request alone is insufficient: the atomic durable effect-and-key invariant is the essential premise.

reasoning_steps.title: Turn the counterexample into a controlled mechanism test
reasoning_steps.argument: First test all seven terminal paths using a deterministic fault injector at the commit/acknowledgment boundary. Require the ledger and acknowledgment records to match the enumeration before estimating stochastic effects. Then compare the three architectures over isolated, randomly assigned instances, using shared pre-generated fault schedules for paired comparisons where the coupling is meaningful. At a=0.7, b=0.2, c=0.1, the model predicts the ordering idempotent retry > baseline > non-idempotent retry for ledger correctness, but both retry arms > baseline for acknowledged completion. Vary b below, at, and above c to test the predicted sign reversal. Report paired uncertainty for correctness differences, not just separate success percentages. This is a proposed falsifiable test; its results are unknown.

reasoning_steps.title: Bound the architectural conclusion
reasoning_steps.argument: The analysis isolates one mechanism: uncertainty about whether a state-changing action committed. It demonstrates that retry count and acknowledgment rate are insufficient reliability measures, and that a particular deduplication invariant removes duplicate effects in this model. It does not establish the superiority of an implemented agent architecture. Real retry outcomes may be correlated; deduplication may expire or fail; several external effects may not share a transaction; and stopping or querying status may consume a deadline. Those conditions require new models and experiments rather than transfer of the numerical results.

assumptions: The task is exactly one externally applied debit for one logical request; correctness is determined from authoritative external state, not acknowledgment alone.
Each non-idempotent invocation has mutually exclusive A/B/C outcomes with fixed probabilities a,b,c summing to one; successive outcomes are independent.
Acknowledgments are authentic and correspond to an accepted operation. Both lost acknowledgments and pre-commit failures are observed as timeouts.
The retry policy makes at most two invocations, retries only after timeout, and performs no status query, compensation, or concurrent action.

The idempotent comparison additionally assumes an atomic, durable server-side association between the logical key, fixed payload, applied effect, and retrievable result, with no key expiry during the task.
The numerical example uses a=0.7, b=0.2, c=0.1 as illustrative model parameters, not estimated environmental frequencies.

strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

output.claim: A defensible lower confidence bound on agent reliability must account separately for task-level sampling uncertainty and false acceptance by the completion oracle. Under the explicit sampling and adjudication assumptions below, let q_hat be the mean oracle-pass fraction across N independent task clusters, and let f_U be a one-sided upper confidence bound on the joint probability of oracle acceptance and actual failure, estimated from an independent audit panel. Then L = max(0, q_hat - sqrt(log(2/alpha)/(2N)) - f_U) is a valid lower confidence bound for actual end-to-end success with coverage at least 1-alpha. Arbitrarily many repeated executions of the same tasks cannot generally replace additional independently sampled tasks in this guarantee.
output.method: Develop a finite-sample measurement lemma and a counterexample to treating repeated executions as independent task evidence. Hypothesis: task clustering and false acceptance can each make nominal benchmark confidence substantially overstate evidence for actual reliability. The discriminating counterexample fixes execution outcomes within each task while varying task difficulty; a run-level binomial analysis then fails its advertised coverage. The proposed empirical test compares naive run-level intervals with the task-level, oracle-corrected bound over repeated independently generated evaluation panels, including a control with no task heterogeneity and a condition with oracle false acceptance. This test has not been executed. The analytical guarantee assumes independently sampled task clusters, an unchanged evaluation protocol, distribution-matched audits, and correct reference adjudication. No runtime or external literature was available; the contribution is a mathematical protocol component, not a measured improvement in any agent.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the deployment-scoped reliability estimand
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix a task distribution D, agent/model/prompt versions, tool interfaces, environment-generation policy, and execution budget. For a sampled task, execute a prespecified batch of r runs. Select an index J uniformly from those r runs. Let Y_J be 1 exactly when the selected run satisfies the independently specified end-state requirements, safety constraints, and deadline; otherwise it is 0. The estimand is p = E[Y_J]. Let Z_J be the automated completion oracle's binary acceptance decision. This definition measures success per attempted execution under the batch protocol, not success conditional on acceptance, success after unlimited retries, or success of a fresh isolated execution unless that is the specified protocol. Timeouts and crashes remain attempted executions.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate actual success from oracle acceptance
reasoning_steps.argument: Define q = P(Z_J=1), f = P(Z_J=1,Y_J=0), and g = P(Z_J=0,Y_J=1). Partitioning the four possible values of (Y_J,Z_J) gives p = q - f + g, hence p >= q-f. Thus oracle pass rate alone does not identify actual success. For example, Z_J=1 always is compatible both with Y_J=1 always and with Y_J=0 always. Both systems have q=1, but their actual reliability is respectively 1 and 0. The correction f is a joint false-acceptance probability, not the different quantity P(Z_J=1 | Y_J=0).

reasoning_steps.title: Use independent task clusters as the concentration units
reasoning_steps.argument: For evaluation task i, define X_i = (1/r) sum over j of Z_ij. Under independent task-cluster sampling and independent cluster-level execution randomness, X_1 through X_N are independent random variables in [0,1], with E[X_i]=q. Dependence between runs within a task is unrestricted. Set q_hat = (1/N) sum_i X_i. Hoeffding's inequality gives P(q < q_hat-t) <= exp(-2Nt^2). Choosing t = sqrt(log(2/alpha)/(2N)) therefore gives q >= q_hat-t except on an event of probability at most alpha/2. This conservative guarantee does not require within-task independence and consequently does not gain a factor r in its exponent.

reasoning_steps.title: Estimate false acceptance with a distribution-matched reference audit
reasoning_steps.argument: Independently sample m audit tasks from D and execute the same r-run protocol on each. On each audit task select one run uniformly at random and adjudicate its true outcome using the reference procedure. Let A_l = 1 when that selected run has Z=1 and Y=0, and 0 otherwise. The A_l are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter f, so K = sum_l A_l is Binomial(m,f). Put delta=alpha/2. For observed K=k<m, define f_U as the unique u in (0,1) satisfying sum from j=0 to k of binom(m,j) u^j (1-u)^(m-j) = delta; for k=m set f_U=1. Inverting the lower-tail binomial test gives P(f<=f_U)>=1-delta. Its coverage is conservative because of discreteness. Adjudicating just one selected run reduces reference-review work, but does not justify omitting other batch runs if they change the selected run's outcome distribution.

reasoning_steps.title: Combine the two uncertainty sources
reasoning_steps.argument: With probability at least 1-alpha, both q >= q_hat-t and f <= f_U hold, by the union bound. On that event, p >= q-f >= q_hat-t-f_U. Since p is nonnegative, L = max(0,q_hat-t-f_U) is a valid lower bound. The audit and evaluation panels were specified as independent for a clean protocol; the union-bound step itself does not require independence between their confidence events. The statement covers sampling uncertainty only under the stated task distribution and protocol. It does not certify distribution shift, erroneous reference labels, or future adaptive changes to the agent.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why repeated trials can produce false confidence
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider a population with equal probabilities of an easy task and a hard task. Every execution on an easy task succeeds and every execution on a hard task fails, with a perfect oracle. Thus p=q=1/2. Evaluate N=1 sampled task r=100 times. With probability 1/2, all 100 executions succeed. A naive one-sided 95% binomial lower bound treating those runs as independent would then be 0.05^(1/100), which is greater than 1/2 because 0.05 > 2^(-100). Consequently that procedure excludes the true p on an event of probability at least 1/2, rather than at most 0.05. This is a mathematical counterexample to the independence assumption, not an empirical finding about a particular benchmark. Repeating tasks remains useful for estimating within-task variability; it does not create new independent samples of task difficulty.

reasoning_steps.title: Translate zero observed false acceptances into an audit requirement
reasoning_steps.argument: When K=0, the audit bound simplifies to f_U = 1-delta^(1/m). It is positive for every finite m. To obtain f_U <= epsilon after observing zero false acceptances, with 0<epsilon<1, the fixed audit size must satisfy m >= ceil(log(delta)/log(1-epsilon)). This calculation specifies an audit-size requirement conditional on observing no errors; it does not promise that the audit will observe none. The evaluator must fix the sample size in advance or use a separately justified sequential confidence procedure rather than stopping opportunistically when this bound looks favorable.

reasoning_steps.title: Turn the lemma into a reproducible evaluation module
reasoning_steps.argument: Before evaluation, register the task population, sampling unit, r, N, m, alpha, success rubric, budget, timeout policy, and reference-adjudication process. Isolate task state and document any shared services that could violate cluster independence. Retain task identifiers, run seeds, versions, external-state snapshots where feasible, tool traces, oracle decisions, adjudication records, resource consumption, and all failed attempts. Report q_hat, K/m, f_U, and L alongside task-stratum outcomes and severe-failure counts. Report per-attempt cost and observed aggregate cost per verified success separately; the bound concerns success probability, not economic optimality. Do not apply this formula unchanged to oversampled strata with unequal weights, selected subsets, or simultaneous claims across many metrics.

assumptions: The target is the explicitly defined fixed-protocol reliability p for a task drawn from D and a uniformly selected run within its r-run batch.

Evaluation task clusters are independently and identically sampled from D, with independent cluster-level execution randomness and no unmodeled cross-task state dependence; within-task dependence is unrestricted.
Audit tasks are independently drawn from the same D and use the same execution protocol and uniform run-selection mechanism as the target estimand.
Reference adjudication correctly determines Y for each selected audited execution. Merely using another similar model as a judge does not establish this premise.
The execution policy, versions, budgets, rubric, sampling plan, sample sizes, and confidence level are fixed before examining evaluation outcomes.
All attempted executions are retained, and sampling, execution failures, or missing logs do not selectively remove difficult cases.

output.claim: Under an explicit ambiguous-commit model, recovery using only the agent's local checkpoint cannot guarantee exactly one external effect. If an uncommitted request and a committed request with a lost acknowledgment produce identical local observations, any policy forced to choose between skipping and retrying has worst-case error probability at least 1/2. This is a conditional theoretical result, not an observed agent failure rate. It identifies a concrete boundary: restoring local state is not sufficient to restore consistency with external state.
output.method: Derive an indistinguishability bound for a non-idempotent external action, then specify a controlled fault-injection experiment. Hypothesis: ambiguous external commits cause an unavoidable missing-effect/duplicate-effect tradeoff for local-only recovery, whereas durable atomic deduplication with stable operation identity removes this particular ambiguity under stated assumptions. The discriminating outcome is externally audited effect count, not an agent's completion statement. Compare skipped retry, unconditional retry, checkpoint-and-retry, and stable-key deduplicated retry under matched pre-commit loss and post-commit acknowledgment loss. Include no-fault controls, fixed task/model/prompt versions, paired environment snapshots and seeds, identical resource caps, and separately reported realized costs. Neither runtime is available, so no experiment was executed. The proposed empirical comparison must not be interpreted as a measured benefit.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the operation, objective, and observation boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider an agent instructed to cause exactly one irreversible external effect, such as appending one shipment order. Each accepted ordinary request creates one effect; there is no built-in deduplication. Let N be the external effect count for this task. Correctness is N=1, not merely receiving a plausible response. The agent records the same local intent before sending the request. At a timeout, its accessible checkpoint, messages, and observations do not reveal whether that request committed. Assume the only terminal recovery choices are skip or one retry; the retry, if chosen, commits exactly one additional effect. This intentionally restricted model isolates ambiguous-commit recovery rather than arbitrary tool or model errors.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct two indistinguishable fault histories
reasoning_steps.argument: In history H0, the initial request is lost before commitment, leaving N=0. In history H1, the request commits, leaving N=1, but its acknowledgment is lost. Both histories end at the same timeout with the same local intent record and no acknowledgment. By assumption, no authoritative status lookup or other distinguishing observation is available before the decision. Therefore a policy using only that local information must use the same retry probability q in both histories. Random internal reasoning or replanning cannot distinguish two histories when its inputs and randomization distribution are identical.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the sharp worst-case error bound
reasoning_steps.argument: In H0, skipping leaves N=0 and retrying yields N=1, so the error probability is e0=1-q. In H1, skipping preserves N=1 and retrying yields N=2, so e1=q. Consequently e0+e1=1 and max(e0,e1)>=1/2. Equality is attained by q=1/2, making the bound sharp within this model. The deterministic edge cases q=0 and q=1 each fail with probability one in one history. This is a worst-case bound over two possible histories, not an assertion that either history occurs equally often in deployment.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate worst-case reliability from deployment-average reliability
reasoning_steps.argument: If H1 has known conditional probability p among ambiguous timeouts, expected error is (1-p)(1-q)+pq. This affine function is minimized at q=1 when p<1/2, at q=0 when p>1/2, and by any q when p=1/2. The minimum is min(p,1-p). Thus an excellent average result can coexist with certain failure in the rarer history. The expression applies only within the ambiguous-timeout population and with equal weighting of missing and duplicate effects; it is not an overall task failure rate or an appropriate loss function when duplicate effects are more harmful.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain the failure chain and limits of checkpoint recovery
reasoning_steps.argument: The initiating fault is request or acknowledgment loss. The propagation chain is ambiguous external commitment, followed by a recovery decision from indistinguishable local state, followed by either a missing effect or duplicate effect. If the agent treats restored local control flow as proof of completed external work, it can additionally produce a false completion claim. Rolling back only the local checkpoint does not decrement N, so it does not invalidate the indistinguishability argument. This locates the problem at the tool/state boundary rather than demonstrating a reasoning deficit in the model. Escalation, indefinite waiting, authoritative lookup, compensation, and refusing to claim completion fall outside the forced-choice theorem; they can change safety or completion outcomes and must be evaluated separately.

reasoning_steps.title: State a sufficient repair for this model, with its assumptions
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose instead the agent durably records a unique operation key k and payload before the first send, retains both across recovery, and reuses them on every retry. Suppose the external service atomically couples the effect with a durable record k->result: an unseen key creates one effect and its record, while an already recorded key returns the recorded result without another effect. The record survives for the entire retry horizon, keys are not reused across distinct operations, and at least one request eventually reaches the service. In H0, the delivered retry sees an unseen key and creates one effect. In H1, it sees the recorded key and creates none. Hence both histories end with N=1. Atomic coupling is essential: recording the key separately from the effect can leave either a recorded-but-missing effect or an unrecorded duplicate opportunity. This establishes a sufficient condition for effect count in the toy model, not a general guarantee of verified completion, arbitrary payload correctness, or timely termination.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the discriminating experiment and independent oracle
reasoning_steps.argument: Use an instrumented append-only service with an evaluator-only committed-event ledger. Inject either loss before commitment or acknowledgment loss after commitment; ensure the agent-visible timeout and checkpoint are identical across the paired cases. Test skip, unconditional ordinary retry, local-checkpoint ordinary retry, and stable-key atomic-deduplication retry. Under the model, predicted effect-count pairs (H0,H1) are respectively (0,1), (1,2), (1,2), and (1,1); these are derived predictions, not execution results. Add no-fault controls to detect implementation defects unrelated to recovery. Verify the observation equivalence from captured agent-visible inputs and verify actual retry choices from traces rather than assuming policy compliance. The primary outcomes are missing-effect and duplicate-effect rates from the private ledger. Secondary outcomes are false completion, unresolved/escalated tasks, time to verified completion, requests, tokens, latency, and monetary cost. Include every assigned trial, including budget exhaustion; do not condition comparisons on successful recovery.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate protocol validation from agent-level evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: First validate the injection harness with scripted policies, for which the preceding effect-count predictions are exact under the assumptions. Then evaluate agent-controlled recovery on the same paired scenarios across repeated seeds and held-out task wrappers. Randomize treatment assignment and trial order within task blocks; pin model, prompt, tool schema, environment snapshot, and budget caps. Report outcomes by fault location as well as any deployment-weighted aggregate, with task-clustered uncertainty when multiple seeds share a task. Repeat with acknowledgment delays, concurrent workers, crashes around deduplication boundaries, and retry horizons exceeding key retention. These extensions test where the sufficient conditions break; they are not covered by the proof. A textual critic sharing the same missing external information cannot independently certify N=1 merely by agreeing with the agent.

assumptions: The task requires exactly one external effect; zero and multiple effects are incorrect.
The initial request either never commits or commits once with its acknowledgment lost, and these cases have identical agent-accessible observations at recovery.
The ordinary operation is non-idempotent, and local rollback cannot undo its external effect.

For the lower bound, the agent must terminate by skipping or issuing exactly one retry; that retry commits one additional effect. No authoritative lookup, compensation, or escalation is available within this decision model.

For the sufficient-repair result only, stable operation identity and payload survive recovery; the external service atomically and durably deduplicates effects by that identity for the entire retry horizon; distinct operations do not collide; and at least one request is delivered.

output.claim: In an explicit partial-commit model, adding one retry can increase acknowledged completion while decreasing actual task correctness. If an attempt applies an operation and returns an acknowledgment with probability a, applies it but loses the acknowledgment with probability b, and does nothing and times out with probability c, then retrying once after a timeout changes the probability of exactly one applied operation by (a+b)(c-b). Thus, when b>c and a+b>0, retries reduce correctness despite increasing acknowledged completion whenever 0<a<1. This is a conditional analytical counterexample, not an empirical finding about deployed agents.
output.method: Analyze a minimal state-changing tool task: apply exactly one debit. Compare three architectures: no retry; one retry after timeout without deduplication; and the same retry policy with atomic, durable server-side idempotency. Derive the terminal outcomes by exhaustive case analysis. Hypothesis: acknowledgment-based evaluation can rank a retry mechanism above a baseline even when an independent ledger oracle ranks it below. The discriminating experiment would inject separately controlled pre-commit failures and post-commit acknowledgment losses, randomize architectures across isolated task instances, and compare acknowledgment, ledger correctness, duplicate effects, latency, and cost. The calculation assumes independent identically distributed attempt outcomes, reliable acknowledgments, no concurrent writers, and no compensating operations. No experiment was executed; both supplied computational runtimes are unavailable.

reasoning_steps.title: Define task correctness separately from reported completion
reasoning_steps.argument: Let N be the number of applied debits for one logical request. Actual correctness is Y=1 exactly when N=1, regardless of what the agent reports. Reported completion is R=1 when the agent receives at least one valid acknowledgment. N=0 is omission; N>=2 is duplication. A read-only oracle inspecting an authoritative ledger can evaluate Y after execution. This deliberately narrow task makes the correctness predicate explicit rather than treating fluent completion reports as evidence.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the failure model and baseline
reasoning_steps.argument: Each attempted invocation has one of three mutually exclusive outcomes: A, one operation applied and acknowledged, with probability a; B, one operation applied but acknowledgment lost, with probability b; C, no operation applied and timeout, with probability c. Here a,b,c>=0 and a+b+c=1. Outcomes of successive invocations are independent with the same probabilities. The baseline invokes once. Therefore P(Y=1)=a+b, P(R=1)=a, and duplicate probability is zero. A B outcome is a correct external state with unresolved client knowledge, not a false claim of completion.

reasoning_steps.title: Enumerate the non-idempotent retry outcomes
reasoning_steps.argument: The retry policy stops after A and invokes once more after B or C. Its terminal paths are A, BA, BB, BC, CA, CB, and CC, with probabilities a, ba, b², bc, ca, cb, and c². These exhaust all outcomes because their sum is a+(b+c)(a+b+c)=1. Exactly one operation occurs on A, BC, CA, and CB. Two operations occur on BA and BB. No operation occurs on CC. Acknowledgment occurs on A, BA, and CA.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the ranking reversal and its boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: For the retry policy, P(Y=1)=a+ca+2bc, P(R=1)=a+(b+c)a=a(2-a), and P(N>=2)=b(a+b). Subtracting baseline correctness gives a+ca+2bc-(a+b)=(a+b)(c-b). Thus retries harm correctness when post-commit acknowledgment loss is more frequent than pre-commit failure, provided a+b>0. Reported completion increases by a(1-a), strictly positive for 0<a<1. The formulas also cover edge cases: b=c gives no correctness change; a=1 causes no retry; c=1 leaves correctness zero. No claim follows that retries are generally harmful outside these assumptions.

reasoning_steps.title: Give a concrete analytical counterexample
reasoning_steps.argument: Set a=7/10, b=2/10, c=1/10. The baseline has actual correctness 0.90 and acknowledged completion 0.70. One non-idempotent retry has actual correctness 0.81, acknowledged completion 0.91, duplicate probability 0.18, and omission probability 0.01. Its probability of acknowledged but incorrect completion is P(BA)=0.14. Expected invocation count rises from 1 to 1+(b+c)=1.30. These numbers are substitutions into the proved formulas, not simulated or observed rates. They show a 21-percentage-point gain in acknowledged completion alongside a 9-percentage-point loss in actual correctness.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify the invariant needed for the revised architecture
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose every retry carries the same logical operation key and payload, and a server atomically and durably records that key together with its effect. Repeated accepted requests for the key return the prior result without applying another debit. Within the same A/B/C transport model, interpret A and B as acceptance of the logical operation, either initially or by retrieving its prior result. This invariant ensures N<=1. Under the retry policy N=0 only on CC, so P(Y=1)=1-c², while P(R=1)=a(2-a) remains unchanged. For the example, correctness is 0.99 and duplication is zero. A key in the client request alone is insufficient: the atomic durable effect-and-key invariant is the essential premise.

reasoning_steps.title: Turn the counterexample into a controlled mechanism test
reasoning_steps.argument: First test all seven terminal paths using a deterministic fault injector at the commit/acknowledgment boundary. Require the ledger and acknowledgment records to match the enumeration before estimating stochastic effects. Then compare the three architectures over isolated, randomly assigned instances, using shared pre-generated fault schedules for paired comparisons where the coupling is meaningful. At a=0.7, b=0.2, c=0.1, the model predicts the ordering idempotent retry > baseline > non-idempotent retry for ledger correctness, but both retry arms > baseline for acknowledged completion. Vary b below, at, and above c to test the predicted sign reversal. Report paired uncertainty for correctness differences, not just separate success percentages. This is a proposed falsifiable test; its results are unknown.

reasoning_steps.title: Bound the architectural conclusion
reasoning_steps.argument: The analysis isolates one mechanism: uncertainty about whether a state-changing action committed. It demonstrates that retry count and acknowledgment rate are insufficient reliability measures, and that a particular deduplication invariant removes duplicate effects in this model. It does not establish the superiority of an implemented agent architecture. Real retry outcomes may be correlated; deduplication may expire or fail; several external effects may not share a transaction; and stopping or querying status may consume a deadline. Those conditions require new models and experiments rather than transfer of the numerical results.

assumptions: The task is exactly one externally applied debit for one logical request; correctness is determined from authoritative external state, not acknowledgment alone.
Each non-idempotent invocation has mutually exclusive A/B/C outcomes with fixed probabilities a,b,c summing to one; successive outcomes are independent.
Acknowledgments are authentic and correspond to an accepted operation. Both lost acknowledgments and pre-commit failures are observed as timeouts.
The retry policy makes at most two invocations, retries only after timeout, and performs no status query, compensation, or concurrent action.

The idempotent comparison additionally assumes an atomic, durable server-side association between the logical key, fixed payload, applied effect, and retrievable result, with no key expiry during the task.
The numerical example uses a=0.7, b=0.2, c=0.1 as illustrative model parameters, not estimated environmental frequencies.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the deployment-scoped reliability estimand
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix a task distribution D, agent/model/prompt versions, tool interfaces, environment-generation policy, and execution budget. For a sampled task, execute a prespecified batch of r runs. Select an index J uniformly from those r runs. Let Y_J be 1 exactly when the selected run satisfies the independently specified end-state requirements, safety constraints, and deadline; otherwise it is 0. The estimand is p = E[Y_J]. Let Z_J be the automated completion oracle's binary acceptance decision. This definition measures success per attempted execution under the batch protocol, not success conditional on acceptance, success after unlimited retries, or success of a fresh isolated execution unless that is the specified protocol. Timeouts and crashes remain attempted executions.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate actual success from oracle acceptance
reasoning_steps.argument: Define q = P(Z_J=1), f = P(Z_J=1,Y_J=0), and g = P(Z_J=0,Y_J=1). Partitioning the four possible values of (Y_J,Z_J) gives p = q - f + g, hence p >= q-f. Thus oracle pass rate alone does not identify actual success. For example, Z_J=1 always is compatible both with Y_J=1 always and with Y_J=0 always. Both systems have q=1, but their actual reliability is respectively 1 and 0. The correction f is a joint false-acceptance probability, not the different quantity P(Z_J=1 | Y_J=0).

reasoning_steps.title: Use independent task clusters as the concentration units
reasoning_steps.argument: For evaluation task i, define X_i = (1/r) sum over j of Z_ij. Under independent task-cluster sampling and independent cluster-level execution randomness, X_1 through X_N are independent random variables in [0,1], with E[X_i]=q. Dependence between runs within a task is unrestricted. Set q_hat = (1/N) sum_i X_i. Hoeffding's inequality gives P(q < q_hat-t) <= exp(-2Nt^2). Choosing t = sqrt(log(2/alpha)/(2N)) therefore gives q >= q_hat-t except on an event of probability at most alpha/2. This conservative guarantee does not require within-task independence and consequently does not gain a factor r in its exponent.

reasoning_steps.title: Estimate false acceptance with a distribution-matched reference audit
reasoning_steps.argument: Independently sample m audit tasks from D and execute the same r-run protocol on each. On each audit task select one run uniformly at random and adjudicate its true outcome using the reference procedure. Let A_l = 1 when that selected run has Z=1 and Y=0, and 0 otherwise. The A_l are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter f, so K = sum_l A_l is Binomial(m,f). Put delta=alpha/2. For observed K=k<m, define f_U as the unique u in (0,1) satisfying sum from j=0 to k of binom(m,j) u^j (1-u)^(m-j) = delta; for k=m set f_U=1. Inverting the lower-tail binomial test gives P(f<=f_U)>=1-delta. Its coverage is conservative because of discreteness. Adjudicating just one selected run reduces reference-review work, but does not justify omitting other batch runs if they change the selected run's outcome distribution.

reasoning_steps.title: Combine the two uncertainty sources
reasoning_steps.argument: With probability at least 1-alpha, both q >= q_hat-t and f <= f_U hold, by the union bound. On that event, p >= q-f >= q_hat-t-f_U. Since p is nonnegative, L = max(0,q_hat-t-f_U) is a valid lower bound. The audit and evaluation panels were specified as independent for a clean protocol; the union-bound step itself does not require independence between their confidence events. The statement covers sampling uncertainty only under the stated task distribution and protocol. It does not certify distribution shift, erroneous reference labels, or future adaptive changes to the agent.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why repeated trials can produce false confidence
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider a population with equal probabilities of an easy task and a hard task. Every execution on an easy task succeeds and every execution on a hard task fails, with a perfect oracle. Thus p=q=1/2. Evaluate N=1 sampled task r=100 times. With probability 1/2, all 100 executions succeed. A naive one-sided 95% binomial lower bound treating those runs as independent would then be 0.05^(1/100), which is greater than 1/2 because 0.05 > 2^(-100). Consequently that procedure excludes the true p on an event of probability at least 1/2, rather than at most 0.05. This is a mathematical counterexample to the independence assumption, not an empirical finding about a particular benchmark. Repeating tasks remains useful for estimating within-task variability; it does not create new independent samples of task difficulty.

reasoning_steps.title: Translate zero observed false acceptances into an audit requirement
reasoning_steps.argument: When K=0, the audit bound simplifies to f_U = 1-delta^(1/m). It is positive for every finite m. To obtain f_U <= epsilon after observing zero false acceptances, with 0<epsilon<1, the fixed audit size must satisfy m >= ceil(log(delta)/log(1-epsilon)). This calculation specifies an audit-size requirement conditional on observing no errors; it does not promise that the audit will observe none. The evaluator must fix the sample size in advance or use a separately justified sequential confidence procedure rather than stopping opportunistically when this bound looks favorable.

Report per-attempt cost and observed aggregate cost per verified success separately; the bound concerns success probability, not economic optimality. Do not apply this formula unchanged to oversampled strata with unequal weights, selected subsets, or simultaneous claims across many metrics.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the deployment-scoped reliability estimand
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix a task distribution D, agent/model/prompt versions, tool interfaces, environment-generation policy, and execution budget. For a sampled task, execute a prespecified batch of r runs. Select an index J uniformly from those r runs. Let Y_J be 1 exactly when the selected run satisfies the independently specified end-state requirements, safety constraints, and deadline; otherwise it is 0. The estimand is p = E[Y_J]. Let Z_J be the automated completion oracle's binary acceptance decision. This definition measures success per attempted execution under the batch protocol, not success conditional on acceptance, success after unlimited retries, or success of a fresh isolated execution unless that is the specified protocol. Timeouts and crashes remain attempted executions.

review.rationale: The uniform run selection makes E[Y_J] the expected within-batch success fraction under the fixed protocol. Explicitly including crashes and timeouts avoids conditioning on successful execution or oracle acceptance. This defines an estimand rather than establishing deployment representativeness.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate actual success from oracle acceptance
reasoning_steps.argument: Define q = P(Z_J=1), f = P(Z_J=1,Y_J=0), and g = P(Z_J=0,Y_J=1). Partitioning the four possible values of (Y_J,Z_J) gives p = q - f + g, hence p >= q-f. Thus oracle pass rate alone does not identify actual success. For example, Z_J=1 always is compatible both with Y_J=1 always and with Y_J=0 always. Both systems have q=1, but their actual reliability is respectively 1 and 0. The correction f is a joint false-acceptance probability, not the different quantity P(Z_J=1 | Y_J=0).

review.rationale: Partitioning the joint binary outcomes gives q=P(Y=1,Z=1)+f and p=P(Y=1,Z=1)+g, so p=q-f+g. The two constant-oracle examples correctly demonstrate nonidentification from q alone, and f is correctly distinguished from a conditional false-positive rate.

reasoning_steps.title: Use independent task clusters as the concentration units
reasoning_steps.argument: For evaluation task i, define X_i = (1/r) sum over j of Z_ij. Under independent task-cluster sampling and independent cluster-level execution randomness, X_1 through X_N are independent random variables in [0,1], with E[X_i]=q. Dependence between runs within a task is unrestricted. Set q_hat = (1/N) sum_i X_i. Hoeffding's inequality gives P(q < q_hat-t) <= exp(-2Nt^2). Choosing t = sqrt(log(2/alpha)/(2N)) therefore gives q >= q_hat-t except on an event of probability at most alpha/2. This conservative guarantee does not require within-task independence and consequently does not gain a factor r in its exponent.

review.rationale: Under the listed independent-cluster assumptions, each X_i lies in [0,1] and has expectation q because uniform run selection averages the r oracle decisions. One-sided Hoeffding therefore has exponent 2Nt^2. Dependence among runs within X_i does not invalidate that application or justify an Nr exponent.

reasoning_steps.title: Estimate false acceptance with a distribution-matched reference audit
reasoning_steps.argument: Independently sample m audit tasks from D and execute the same r-run protocol on each. On each audit task select one run uniformly at random and adjudicate its true outcome using the reference procedure. Let A_l = 1 when that selected run has Z=1 and Y=0, and 0 otherwise. The A_l are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter f, so K = sum_l A_l is Binomial(m,f). Put delta=alpha/2. For observed K=k<m, define f_U as the unique u in (0,1) satisfying sum from j=0 to k of binom(m,j) u^j (1-u)^(m-j) = delta; for k=m set f_U=1. Inverting the lower-tail binomial test gives P(f<=f_U)>=1-delta. Its coverage is conservative because of discreteness. Adjudicating just one selected run reduces reference-review work, but does not justify omitting other batch runs if they change the selected run's outcome distribution.

review.rationale: Distribution-matched independent audit clusters, uniform run selection, and correct adjudication make the A_l independent Bernoulli(f). For k<m, the binomial lower-tail probability decreases continuously from 1 to 0 as u increases, giving the stated unique root. Inversion yields the conservative one-sided upper confidence limit, including f_U=1 at k=m.

reasoning_steps.title: Combine the two uncertainty sources
reasoning_steps.argument: With probability at least 1-alpha, both q >= q_hat-t and f <= f_U hold, by the union bound. On that event, p >= q-f >= q_hat-t-f_U. Since p is nonnegative, L = max(0,q_hat-t-f_U) is a valid lower bound. The audit and evaluation panels were specified as independent for a clean protocol; the union-bound step itself does not require independence between their confidence events. The statement covers sampling uncertainty only under the stated task distribution and protocol. It does not certify distribution shift, erroneous reference labels, or future adaptive changes to the agent.

review.rationale: The union bound limits failure of either confidence event to alpha. On their intersection, p>=q-f>=q_hat-t-f_U, and clipping at zero remains valid because p is nonnegative. Independence between those two events is unnecessary. The stated exclusions correctly preserve the conditional scope.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why repeated trials can produce false confidence
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider a population with equal probabilities of an easy task and a hard task. Every execution on an easy task succeeds and every execution on a hard task fails, with a perfect oracle. Thus p=q=1/2. Evaluate N=1 sampled task r=100 times. With probability 1/2, all 100 executions succeed. A naive one-sided 95% binomial lower bound treating those runs as independent would then be 0.05^(1/100), which is greater than 1/2 because 0.05 > 2^(-100). Consequently that procedure excludes the true p on an event of probability at least 1/2, rather than at most 0.05. This is a mathematical counterexample to the independence assumption, not an empirical finding about a particular benchmark. Repeating tasks remains useful for estimating within-task variability; it does not create new independent samples of task difficulty.

review.rationale: With one sampled task, all r outcomes share its easy/hard status. The all-success event has probability 1/2, while the naive 95% binomial lower endpoint on that event is 0.05^(1/100)>1/2. Thus the procedure's noncoverage probability is at least 1/2 under this construction, contradicting its advertised 5% maximum.

reasoning_steps.title: Translate zero observed false acceptances into an audit requirement
reasoning_steps.argument: When K=0, the audit bound simplifies to f_U = 1-delta^(1/m). It is positive for every finite m. This calculation specifies an audit-size requirement conditional on observing no errors; it does not promise that the audit will observe none. The evaluator must fix the sample size in advance or use a separately justified sequential confidence procedure rather than stopping opportunistically when this bound looks favorable.

artifacts.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
artifacts.claim_or_question: Under an explicit ambiguous-commit model, recovery using only the agent's local checkpoint cannot guarantee exactly one external effect. If an uncommitted request and a committed request with a lost acknowledgment produce identical local observations, any policy forced to choose between skipping and retrying has worst-case error probability at least 1/2. This is a conditional theoretical result, not an observed agent failure rate. It identifies a concrete boundary: restoring local state is not sufficient to restore consistency with external state.
artifacts.method: Derive an indistinguishability bound for a non-idempotent external action, then specify a controlled fault-injection experiment. Hypothesis: ambiguous external commits cause an unavoidable missing-effect/duplicate-effect tradeoff for local-only recovery, whereas durable atomic deduplication with stable operation identity removes this particular ambiguity under stated assumptions. The discriminating outcome is externally audited effect count, not an agent's completion statement. Compare skipped retry, unconditional retry, checkpoint-and-retry, and stable-key deduplicated retry under matched pre-commit loss and post-commit acknowledgment loss. Include no-fault controls, fixed task/model/prompt versions, paired environment snapshots and seeds, identical resource caps, and separately reported realized costs. Neither runtime is available, so no experiment was executed. The proposed empirical comparison must not be interpreted as a measured benefit.
assumptions: The task requires exactly one external effect; zero and multiple effects are incorrect.
The initial request either never commits or commits once with its acknowledgment lost, and these cases have identical agent-accessible observations at recovery.
The ordinary operation is non-idempotent, and local rollback cannot undo its external effect.

For the lower bound, the agent must terminate by skipping or issuing exactly one retry; that retry commits one additional effect. No authoritative lookup, compensation, or escalation is available within this decision model.

For the sufficient-repair result only, stable operation identity and payload survive recovery; the external service atomically and durably deduplicates effects by that identity for the entire retry horizon; distinct operations do not collide; and at least one request is delivered.

investigator_output.claim: Under an explicit ambiguous-commit model, recovery using only the agent's local checkpoint cannot guarantee exactly one external effect. If an uncommitted request and a committed request with a lost acknowledgment produce identical local observations, any policy forced to choose between skipping and retrying has worst-case error probability at least 1/2. This is a conditional theoretical result, not an observed agent failure rate. It identifies a concrete boundary: restoring local state is not sufficient to restore consistency with external state.

Hypothesis: ambiguous external commits cause an unavoidable missing-effect/duplicate-effect tradeoff for local-only recovery, whereas durable atomic deduplication with stable operation identity removes this particular ambiguity under stated assumptions. The discriminating outcome is externally audited effect count, not an agent's completion statement. Compare skipped retry, unconditional retry, checkpoint-and-retry, and stable-key deduplicated retry under matched pre-commit loss and post-commit acknowledgment loss. Include no-fault controls, fixed task/model/prompt versions, paired environment snapshots and seeds, identical resource caps, and separately reported realized costs. Neither runtime is available, so no experiment was executed. The proposed empirical comparison must not be interpreted as a measured benefit.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the operation, objective, and observation boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider an agent instructed to cause exactly one irreversible external effect, such as appending one shipment order. Each accepted ordinary request creates one effect; there is no built-in deduplication. Let N be the external effect count for this task. Correctness is N=1, not merely receiving a plausible response. The agent records the same local intent before sending the request. At a timeout, its accessible checkpoint, messages, and observations do not reveal whether that request committed. Assume the only terminal recovery choices are skip or one retry; the retry, if chosen, commits exactly one additional effect. This intentionally restricted model isolates ambiguous-commit recovery rather than arbitrary tool or model errors.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct two indistinguishable fault histories
reasoning_steps.argument: In history H0, the initial request is lost before commitment, leaving N=0. In history H1, the request commits, leaving N=1, but its acknowledgment is lost. Both histories end at the same timeout with the same local intent record and no acknowledgment. By assumption, no authoritative status lookup or other distinguishing observation is available before the decision. Therefore a policy using only that local information must use the same retry probability q in both histories. Random internal reasoning or replanning cannot distinguish two histories when its inputs and randomization distribution are identical.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the sharp worst-case error bound
reasoning_steps.argument: In H0, skipping leaves N=0 and retrying yields N=1, so the error probability is e0=1-q. In H1, skipping preserves N=1 and retrying yields N=2, so e1=q. Consequently e0+e1=1 and max(e0,e1)>=1/2. Equality is attained by q=1/2, making the bound sharp within this model. The deterministic edge cases q=0 and q=1 each fail with probability one in one history. This is a worst-case bound over two possible histories, not an assertion that either history occurs equally often in deployment.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate worst-case reliability from deployment-average reliability
reasoning_steps.argument: If H1 has known conditional probability p among ambiguous timeouts, expected error is (1-p)(1-q)+pq. This affine function is minimized at q=1 when p<1/2, at q=0 when p>1/2, and by any q when p=1/2. The minimum is min(p,1-p). Thus an excellent average result can coexist with certain failure in the rarer history. The expression applies only within the ambiguous-timeout population and with equal weighting of missing and duplicate effects; it is not an overall task failure rate or an appropriate loss function when duplicate effects are more harmful.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain the failure chain and limits of checkpoint recovery
reasoning_steps.argument: The initiating fault is request or acknowledgment loss. The propagation chain is ambiguous external commitment, followed by a recovery decision from indistinguishable local state, followed by either a missing effect or duplicate effect. If the agent treats restored local control flow as proof of completed external work, it can additionally produce a false completion claim. Rolling back only the local checkpoint does not decrement N, so it does not invalidate the indistinguishability argument. This locates the problem at the tool/state boundary rather than demonstrating a reasoning deficit in the model. Escalation, indefinite waiting, authoritative lookup, compensation, and refusing to claim completion fall outside the forced-choice theorem; they can change safety or completion outcomes and must be evaluated separately.

reasoning_steps.title: State a sufficient repair for this model, with its assumptions
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose instead the agent durably records a unique operation key k and payload before the first send, retains both across recovery, and reuses them on every retry. Suppose the external service atomically couples the effect with a durable record k->result: an unseen key creates one effect and its record, while an already recorded key returns the recorded result without another effect. The record survives for the entire retry horizon, keys are not reused across distinct operations, and at least one request eventually reaches the service. In H0, the delivered retry sees an unseen key and creates one effect. In H1, it sees the recorded key and creates none. Hence both histories end with N=1. Atomic coupling is essential: recording the key separately from the effect can leave either a recorded-but-missing effect or an unrecorded duplicate opportunity. This establishes a sufficient condition for effect count in the toy model, not a general guarantee of verified completion, arbitrary payload correctness, or timely termination.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the discriminating experiment and independent oracle
reasoning_steps.argument: Use an instrumented append-only service with an evaluator-only committed-event ledger. Inject either loss before commitment or acknowledgment loss after commitment; ensure the agent-visible timeout and checkpoint are identical across the paired cases. Test skip, unconditional ordinary retry, local-checkpoint ordinary retry, and stable-key atomic-deduplication retry. Under the model, predicted effect-count pairs (H0,H1) are respectively (0,1), (1,2), (1,2), and (1,1); these are derived predictions, not execution results. Add no-fault controls to detect implementation defects unrelated to recovery. Verify the observation equivalence from captured agent-visible inputs and verify actual retry choices from traces rather than assuming policy compliance. The primary outcomes are missing-effect and duplicate-effect rates from the private ledger. Secondary outcomes are false completion, unresolved/escalated tasks, time to verified completion, requests, tokens, latency, and monetary cost. Include every assigned trial, including budget exhaustion; do not condition comparisons on successful recovery.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate protocol validation from agent-level evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: First validate the injection harness with scripted policies, for which the preceding effect-count predictions are exact under the assumptions. Then evaluate agent-controlled recovery on the same paired scenarios across repeated seeds and held-out task wrappers. Randomize treatment assignment and trial order within task blocks; pin model, prompt, tool schema, environment snapshot, and budget caps. Report outcomes by fault location as well as any deployment-weighted aggregate, with task-clustered uncertainty when multiple seeds share a task. Repeat with acknowledgment delays, concurrent workers, crashes around deduplication boundaries, and retry horizons exceeding key retention. These extensions test where the sufficient conditions break; they are not covered by the proof. strategy_findings.strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_findings.failure_reason: Provider output exceeded the configured per-call token limit; no artifact was committed
strategy_findings.claim: Conditional on: The target is the explicitly defined fixed-protocol reliability p for a task drawn from D and a uniformly selected run within its r-run batch; Evaluation task clusters are independently and identically sampled from D, with independent cluster-level execution randomness and no unmodeled cross-task state dependence; within-task dependence is unrestricted; Audit tasks are independently drawn from the same D and use the same execution protocol and uniform run-selection mechanism as the target estimand; Reference adjudication correctly determines Y for each selected audited execution. Merely using another similar model as a judge does not establish this premise; The execution policy, versions, budgets, rubric, sampling plan, sample sizes, and confidence level are fixed before examining evaluation outcomes; All attempted executions are retained, and sampling, execution failures, or missing logs do not selectively remove difficult cases. Conditional on the Investigator's listed fixed-protocol, independent-cluster, distribution-matched audit, correct-reference, prespecification, and complete-retention assumptions, and for positive integer N, m, r and 0<alpha<1, L = max(0, q_hat - sqrt(log(2/alpha)/(2N)) - f_U) is a lower confidence bound for the defined reliability p with coverage at least 1-alpha. The cycle-1 counterexample also establishes that increasing repetitions within a task cannot generally replace independently sampled tasks. These local analytical results do not complete the broader evaluation framework or establish real-world reliability.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the deployment-scoped reliability estimand
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix a task distribution D, agent/model/prompt versions, tool interfaces, environment-generation policy, and execution budget. For a sampled task, execute a prespecified batch of r runs. Select an index J uniformly from those r runs. Let Y_J be 1 exactly when the selected run satisfies the independently specified end-state requirements, safety constraints, and deadline; otherwise it is 0. The estimand is p = E[Y_J]. Let Z_J be the automated completion oracle's binary acceptance decision. This definition measures success per attempted execution under the batch protocol, not success conditional on acceptance, success after unlimited retries, or success of a fresh isolated execution unless that is the specified protocol. Timeouts and crashes remain attempted executions.

review.rationale: The uniform run selection makes E[Y_J] the expected within-batch success fraction under the fixed protocol. Explicitly including crashes and timeouts avoids conditioning on successful execution or oracle acceptance. This defines an estimand rather than establishing deployment representativeness.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate actual success from oracle acceptance
reasoning_steps.argument: Define q = P(Z_J=1), f = P(Z_J=1,Y_J=0), and g = P(Z_J=0,Y_J=1). Partitioning the four possible values of (Y_J,Z_J) gives p = q - f + g, hence p >= q-f. Thus oracle pass rate alone does not identify actual success. For example, Z_J=1 always is compatible both with Y_J=1 always and with Y_J=0 always. Both systems have q=1, but their actual reliability is respectively 1 and 0. The correction f is a joint false-acceptance probability, not the different quantity P(Z_J=1 | Y_J=0).

review.rationale: Partitioning the joint binary outcomes gives q=P(Y=1,Z=1)+f and p=P(Y=1,Z=1)+g, so p=q-f+g. The two constant-oracle examples correctly demonstrate nonidentification from q alone, and f is correctly distinguished from a conditional false-positive rate.

reasoning_steps.title: Use independent task clusters as the concentration units
reasoning_steps.argument: For evaluation task i, define X_i = (1/r) sum over j of Z_ij. Under independent task-cluster sampling and independent cluster-level execution randomness, X_1 through X_N are independent random variables in [0,1], with E[X_i]=q. Dependence between runs within a task is unrestricted. Set q_hat = (1/N) sum_i X_i. Hoeffding's inequality gives P(q < q_hat-t) <= exp(-2Nt^2). Choosing t = sqrt(log(2/alpha)/(2N)) therefore gives q >= q_hat-t except on an event of probability at most alpha/2. This conservative guarantee does not require within-task independence and consequently does not gain a factor r in its exponent.

review.rationale: Under the listed independent-cluster assumptions, each X_i lies in [0,1] and has expectation q because uniform run selection averages the r oracle decisions. One-sided Hoeffding therefore has exponent 2Nt^2. Dependence among runs within X_i does not invalidate that application or justify an Nr exponent.

reasoning_steps.title: Estimate false acceptance with a distribution-matched reference audit
reasoning_steps.argument: Independently sample m audit tasks from D and execute the same r-run protocol on each. On each audit task select one run uniformly at random and adjudicate its true outcome using the reference procedure. Let A_l = 1 when that selected run has Z=1 and Y=0, and 0 otherwise. The A_l are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter f, so K = sum_l A_l is Binomial(m,f). Put delta=alpha/2. For observed K=k<m, define f_U as the unique u in (0,1) satisfying sum from j=0 to k of binom(m,j) u^j (1-u)^(m-j) = delta; for k=m set f_U=1. Inverting the lower-tail binomial test gives P(f<=f_U)>=1-delta. Its coverage is conservative because of discreteness. Adjudicating just one selected run reduces reference-review work, but does not justify omitting other batch runs if they change the selected run's outcome distribution.

review.rationale: Distribution-matched independent audit clusters, uniform run selection, and correct adjudication make the A_l independent Bernoulli(f). For k<m, the binomial lower-tail probability decreases continuously from 1 to 0 as u increases, giving the stated unique root. Inversion yields the conservative one-sided upper confidence limit, including f_U=1 at k=m.

reasoning_steps.title: Combine the two uncertainty sources
reasoning_steps.argument: With probability at least 1-alpha, both q >= q_hat-t and f <= f_U hold, by the union bound. On that event, p >= q-f >= q_hat-t-f_U. Since p is nonnegative, L = max(0,q_hat-t-f_U) is a valid lower bound. The audit and evaluation panels were specified as independent for a clean protocol; the union-bound step itself does not require independence between their confidence events. The statement covers sampling uncertainty only under the stated task distribution and protocol. It does not certify distribution shift, erroneous reference labels, or future adaptive changes to the agent.

review.rationale: The union bound limits failure of either confidence event to alpha. On their intersection, p>=q-f>=q_hat-t-f_U, and clipping at zero remains valid because p is nonnegative. Independence between those two events is unnecessary. The stated exclusions correctly preserve the conditional scope.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why repeated trials can produce false confidence
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider a population with equal probabilities of an easy task and a hard task. Every execution on an easy task succeeds and every execution on a hard task fails, with a perfect oracle. Thus p=q=1/2. Evaluate N=1 sampled task r=100 times. With probability 1/2, all 100 executions succeed. A naive one-sided 95% binomial lower bound treating those runs as independent would then be 0.05^(1/100), which is greater than 1/2 because 0.05 > 2^(-100). Consequently that procedure excludes the true p on an event of probability at least 1/2, rather than at most 0.05. This is a mathematical counterexample to the independence assumption, not an empirical finding about a particular benchmark. Repeating tasks remains useful for estimating within-task variability; it does not create new independent samples of task difficulty.

review.rationale: With one sampled task, all r outcomes share its easy/hard status. The all-success event has probability 1/2, while the naive 95% binomial lower endpoint on that event is 0.05^(1/100)>1/2. Thus the procedure's noncoverage probability is at least 1/2 under this construction, contradicting its advertised 5% maximum.

reasoning_steps.title: Translate zero observed false acceptances into an audit requirement
reasoning_steps.argument: When K=0, the audit bound simplifies to f_U = 1-delta^(1/m). It is positive for every finite m. To obtain f_U <= epsilon after observing zero false acceptances, with 0<epsilon<1, the fixed audit size must satisfy m >= ceil(log(delta)/log(1-epsilon)). This calculation specifies an audit-size requirement conditional on observing no errors; it does not promise that the audit will observe none. The evaluator must fix the sample size in advance or use a separately justified sequential confidence procedure rather than stopping opportunistically when this bound looks favorable.

review.rationale: At K=0, the inversion equation is (1-f_U)^m=delta. Solving f_U<=epsilon gives m>=log(delta)/log(1-epsilon), with the integer ceiling as stated. The argument correctly conditions the calculation on observing zero errors and does not authorize optional stopping.

reasoning_steps.title: Turn the lemma into a reproducible evaluation module
reasoning_steps.argument: Before evaluation, register the task population, sampling unit, r, N, m, alpha, success rubric, budget, timeout policy, and reference-adjudication process. Isolate task state and document any shared services that could violate cluster independence. Retain task identifiers, run seeds, versions, external-state snapshots where feasible, tool traces, oracle decisions, adjudication records, resource consumption, and all failed attempts. Report q_hat, K/m, f_U, and L alongside task-stratum outcomes and severe-failure counts. Report per-attempt cost and observed aggregate cost per verified success separately; the bound concerns success probability, not economic optimality. Do not apply this formula unchanged to oversampled strata with unequal weights, selected subsets, or simultaneous claims across many metrics.

review.rationale: The proposed records and prespecification requirements operationalize the assumptions needed by the preceding derivation. The warnings about unequal weighting, selection, and simultaneous claims are appropriate. These are protocol recommendations, not evidence that logging alone establishes independence, reference validity, or economic benefit.
